title: Food and Wine
description: What food does to wine, and the few rules that make a pairing work.
L: Why the same wine tastes different with dinner
Explain why food changes how wine tastes
Name the food elements that matter most
Explain the idea of matching weight

Taste a wine on its own, then with food, and it often changes. A red can turn harsh after a bite of something sweet, or soft after a bite of salty cheese. Pairing isn't about finding a perfect match; it's about avoiding clashes and finding combinations where both taste better.

Your palate adapts to what it has just tasted. After sugar, the next thing tastes less sweet and more sour. After salt, it tastes less bitter and acidic. Fat coats the mouth, so tannin and acidity feel softer and cleaner. These effects are reliable enough to plan around.
The palate adjusts to the last bite
After eating something salty, a wine is likely to seem:
Salt reduces our sense of bitterness and acidity, which is why salty dishes make many wines seem softer and fruitier.

A simple rule that rarely fails: match the weight of the food to the body of the wine. A delicate fish needs a light white; a rich stew needs a fuller red. Big flavours overpower light wines, and big wines flatten delicate food. Colour matters far less than weight.
Light with light, rich with rich
Which of these food elements make a wine seem harder, more bitter or more acidic?
Sweetness and umami make wine feel harsher. Salt and acidity in food make it feel softer.
Food changes how wine tastes, for better or worse
Sugar and umami harden wine; salt and acid soften it
Match the weight of the food to the body of the wine
The two that make wine harder
Explain why sweet food clashes with dry wine
Fix a sweet or umami pairing

Sweetness in food makes a dry wine taste more acidic, more bitter and less fruity. A dry Champagne with a sweet dessert often tastes thin and sour. The rule: the wine should be at least as sweet as the food. That's why sweet wines are served with dessert.
Wine at least as sweet as the food

Umami is the savoury taste of glutamates, found in mushrooms, ripe tomatoes, aged cheese, soy sauce and cured meat. Like sweetness, it makes wine taste more bitter, astringent and acidic, and less fruity. Asparagus and eggs are tricky for the same reason. Salt counteracts it, which is why salty umami dishes are easier to match.
A dry sparkling wine is the ideal match for a very sweet chocolate dessert.
Not true. The sweetness of the dessert makes the dry wine taste sour and thin. A wine at least as sweet as the dessert works far better.

With sweet dishes, choose wines like Sauternes, Tokaji or tawny Port. With umami, reach for fruity, lower-tannin wines, such as Pinot Noir, and add salt or acidity to the dish, like a squeeze of lemon or a little soy. The dish and the wine can both be adjusted.
Sweet wine for sweet; salt for umami
You're serving mushroom risotto. Which wine is the safest choice?
A dry fino Sherry served warm
Umami in mushrooms makes tannin feel harsher, so a fruity, low-tannin red like Pinot Noir handles it best.
Sweet food needs a wine at least as sweet
Umami makes wine more bitter and astringent
Fruity, low-tannin wines and a little salt help with umami
The elements that make wine softer
Explain why acidic food needs acidic wine

Acidic food, like a tomato salad or a dish with lemon, makes a wine taste less acidic, richer and fruitier. But if the wine has lower acidity than the dish, it can taste flat and flabby. So acidic food needs a wine with at least as much acidity, like Sauvignon Blanc or Chianti.

Salt makes wine feel softer and fruitier, which is why salty cheeses and charcuterie are so easy to pair. Bitterness works the other way: bitter food adds to bitterness in the wine. Grilled radicchio or very charred meat can make a tannic red taste harsh, because tannin itself tastes slightly bitter.
Match each food element to its effect on wine.
Salt and acidity soften a wine. Sweetness and bitterness harden it.
Salty blue cheese with a sweet wine, like Roquefort with Sauternes, is one of the great pairings. Salt softens, sweetness balances salt, and the wine's acidity cuts the fat.
A tomato salad with lemon dressing needs a wine with high ____.
Acidic food makes a wine seem less acidic, so the wine needs plenty of acidity to stay fresh.
Acidic food needs wine with at least as much acidity
Salt is wine-friendly, softening and lifting fruit
Bitter food adds to the bitterness of tannic wines
Explain the role of alcohol and tannin

Chilli heat, from capsaicin, is not a taste but a feeling of burning. In the mouth it makes alcohol feel hotter, and it makes tannin and bitterness more aggressive. A high-alcohol, tannic red with a hot curry can feel like fire. The wine also loses fruit.

Sugar and low alcohol calm the burn. Capsaicin dissolves in alcohol and fat, so strong drinks spread it around the mouth. A touch of sweetness and moderate alcohol soothe instead. An off-dry Riesling at 9 or 10% alcohol is a classic match for spicy Thai or Sichuan food.
Off-dry and low alcohol calm the heat
Which wine is the best match for a hot Thai curry?
Lower alcohol and a touch of sugar calm chilli heat. High alcohol and tannin make it burn more.

Fruity, aromatic whites like Gewürztraminer handle spice well. Among reds, choose low-tannin, juicy wines served slightly cool, such as Beaujolais. Fruity rosé also works. Avoid big oak, high alcohol and firm tannin.
Fruity, aromatic, low tannin, moderate alcohol
Which features make a wine harder to pair with chilli?
High alcohol, firm tannin and heavy oak all clash with heat. Sugar and lower alcohol help.
Chilli heat makes alcohol, tannin and bitterness feel stronger
Off-dry, lower-alcohol wines calm the burn
Choose fruity, aromatic, low-tannin wines with spicy food
Analyse a dish before choosing a wine
Pair with confidence for a full meal

Look at the dominant elements, not the main ingredient. Chicken in cream sauce is about fat and richness; chicken with lemon and herbs is about acidity. The sauce, the cooking method and the seasoning often matter more than the meat or fish itself.
Pair the sauce, not the protein

You can match, like a rich oaked Chardonnay with lobster in butter, or contrast, like a crisp Champagne cutting through fried food. High acidity and bubbles act like a squeeze of lemon, cleaning the palate of fat and salt. Tannin works similarly with fatty red meat, which softens it.
Acid and bubbles cut fat; tannin loves fat
Why does a tannic red work well with a fatty steak?
Fat coats the mouth and tannin binds with protein and fat, so each softens the other.
When in doubt, ask where the dish comes from. Regional pairings grew up together over centuries, like Muscadet with oysters or Chianti with tomato-based pasta.
Put the steps of choosing a wine for a dish in order.
Start with what's on the plate, rule out clashes, then fine-tune the style.
Pair the dominant elements, especially the sauce
Match richness or contrast with acidity and bubbles
Regional pairings are a safe starting point
Build a pairing for a dish
Match each food element to its effect on wine.
Sweetness, umami and chilli make wine harder; salt and acidity soften it.
Which wine is best with a sweet dessert?
A wine at least as sweet as the dessert
Sweet food makes dry wine taste thin and sour.
High acidity and bubbles help cut through fried and fatty food.
Yes. They work like a squeeze of lemon, refreshing the palate.
Which wines suit a spicy curry?
Aromatic, off-dry, lower-alcohol whites calm heat. Big, tannic, high-alcohol reds burn.
When choosing a wine, focus on the sauce more than the ____.
The sauce sets the dominant elements, like acid, fat or sweetness.
Sweetness and umami harden wine; salt and acidity soften it
Chilli needs lower alcohol and a touch of sugar
Match weight, then match or contrast the dominant elements
Tannin and fat, acidity and frying, sweet and salty work well together
